name: Working as a Software Engineer
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: How engineering teams really work: agile, tickets, estimates, codebases, design docs, reviews, incidents and growing.

lesson.intro: Passing the interview gets you the job; this pack is about doing it well: scrum and kanban, tickets and estimates, large codebases, design docs, code review, documentation, working with product and design, incidents, communication and growing to mid-level.
objectives: Take part in scrum and kanban, with clear tickets and honest estimates
Find your way around a large codebase
Write design docs, and give and receive useful code reviews
Handle on-call and incidents: escalate early, mitigate first, learn blamelessly
Communicate status, risks and questions in ways that build trust and growth

sections.title: How teams plan work: agile, scrum and kanban
sections.key: Agile teams deliver in small batches: scrum through fixed sprints and events, kanban through continuous flow with work-in-progress limits; most teams mix both.
sections.body:
In your first week you will be invited to sprint planning, a daily standup, backlog refinement and a retro, and someone will ask how many points a ticket is. These rituals come from **agile** development: deliver in small increments, get feedback early, and adjust the plan as you learn.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Most teams run a hybrid: a two-week rhythm, a kanban-style board, standups and retros, with lighter process than the textbook. The intent stays the same: small batches, visible work, regular reflection.

Your part, from week one:

- **Keep your tickets' status current**: the board tells people what is happening without interrupting you.
- **Raise blockers at standup** the day they appear, not at the end of the sprint.
- **Finish before you start**: five half-done tickets deliver nothing.

items.title: Scrum
points: Fixed-length **sprints**, usually two weeks
The **product owner** orders the backlog by value
The **scrum master** keeps the process healthy and removes obstacles
Developers decide how to build

items.title: Kanban
points: No sprints: work flows across a board (To do, In progress, In review, Done)
Each column has a **work-in-progress (WIP) limit**: when review is full, help review instead of starting something new
Watches **cycle time** (start to done for one item) and **throughput** (items finished per week)
Suits unpredictable work: platform, support, operations

visual.title: The events
rows: Pull the most valuable items the team can finish from the ordered backlog, and agree on a sprint goal
About 15 minutes: progress, plans and blockers. Coordination, not problem solving
Clarify, split and estimate upcoming items
Demo what was built to stakeholders and gather feedback
Improve how the team works: what helped, what hurt, one or two concrete changes

sections.pitfall: Turning standup into a status report to the manager or a long debugging session. Keep it short, mention blockers, and move detailed discussions to a follow-up with only the people involved.

activity.title: Measure cycle time
activity.prompt: Kanban teams look at cycle time to spot work that is stuck. Build a dict of ticket id to (done - started).days, print each one, then the average with :.1f, then a list of ids whose cycle time is greater than 7.

props.code:
from datetime import date

tickets = [
    ("API-101", date(2026, 3, 2), date(2026, 3, 4)),
    ("API-102", date(2026, 3, 2), date(2026, 3, 9)),
    ("API-103", date(2026, 3, 3), date(2026, 3, 5)),
    ("API-104", date(2026, 3, 5), date(2026, 3, 16)),
    ("API-105", date(2026, 3, 9), date(2026, 3, 10)),
]   # (id, started, done)

# Cycle time = days from started to done ((done - started).days).
# 1. Print each ticket's cycle time, like: API-101 2
# 2. Print the average with one decimal, like: average 4.6
# 3. Print the ids that took longer than 7 days, as a list.
print(len(tickets), "tickets")
props.task: Print the five cycle times (API-101 2 to API-105 1), then average 4.6, then ['API-104'].
props.expectOutput:
API-101 2
API-102 7
API-103 2
API-104 11
API-105 1
average 4.6
['API-104']

check.question: The In review column on your team's kanban board has hit its WIP limit, and you just finished coding a ticket. What does kanban suggest you do next?
choices: Move your ticket to Done to free a slot
Start the next ticket from To do
Review a teammate's change so work can flow again
Raise the WIP limit
check.explanation: WIP limits make bottlenecks visible and push the team to finish work already in progress. Starting more work while review is jammed only grows the pile.

sections.title: Tickets, estimates and breaking work down
sections.key: A good ticket states the problem and checkable acceptance criteria; split work into vertical slices, estimate the steps including review and deployment, and update estimates early.
sections.body:
A ticket that says "Fix search" can take three times longer than one that says what is broken, for whom, and how you will know it is fixed. Teams track work in Jira, Linear or GitHub Issues, and good tickets share a shape:

[[visual]]

**Break work down** into vertical slices, each small enough to finish and get reviewed in a few days:

[[visual 2]]

**Estimates** help planning; nobody expects them to be exact. Teams use **story points** (relative sizes such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, often chosen by **planning poker** so the first voice does not anchor the room), days, or ticket counts. A big disagreement usually means someone knows about hidden work.

[[visual 3]]

The team's **definition of done** (for example merged, tested, deployed, documented) applies to every ticket, yours included.

layers.label: Context
layers.detail: "pokemon" does not find "Pokémon Red"; 14 support tickets in March. Sometimes a user story: "As a reader, I want..., so that..."

layers.label: Acceptance criteria
layers.detail: Checkable: "POKÉMON" finds it; case and accents ignored; new tests pass; p95 latency stays under 300 ms

layers.label: Links
layers.detail: Designs, logs, related tickets, the original conversation

layers.label: Estimate
layers.detail: 3 points. Unknown: can the database collation do this? Half-day spike first

items.title: Vertical slice
points: Search on one field (author), end to end: database query, API and a basic UI
Works and can ship on its own

items.title: Horizontal layers
points: All the database work, then all the API, then all the UI
Nothing usable until the very end

visual.title: Estimating well
rows: Estimate the steps, not the whole
When they dominate, propose a short, time-boxed **spike** to investigate before committing
Tests, review rounds, migrations and backfills, docs, deployment
On day two, "bigger than we thought because X; three more days" is useful. On the last day it is a surprise

sections.pitfall: Estimating only the coding. Reviews, tests, migrations, docs and deployment are part of done, and leaving them out is the most common reason juniors' estimates slip.

check.question: The team wants to add search to the app. Which first ticket is a vertical slice?
choices: Search books by title only, end to end: query, API endpoint and a basic search box
Write the search API without any way to call it
Design every database table search will ever need
Build the full search UI with mock data
check.explanation: A vertical slice works end to end, so it can be tested, demoed and shipped. Layer-by-layer plans delay all feedback until every layer is done.

sections.title: Reading a large codebase
sections.key: Learn a big codebase by running it, tracing one real request from its entry point, searching for anchors, reading the tests and asking the history why.
sections.body:
Day three: your first ticket is in a repository with 400,000 lines and 30 services. Nobody reads that, and nobody expects you to. You build a map by following real paths through it:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Respect what you do not yet understand: before deleting an odd-looking check, find out why it exists (**Chesterton's fence**). Make your first changes small and well tested.

And ask well. After a focused 15 to 30 minutes, ask with what you found: "I think orders are created in OrderService.place, but I cannot find where the confirmation email is sent. Is it the outbox worker?" One pointer can save you a day.

steps.label: Run it first
steps.detail: Build it, run it locally, pass the tests: setup teaches you the services, database and config

steps.label: Start from an entry point
steps.detail: `main()`, HTTP routes, CLI commands, queue consumers, scheduled jobs: find the one your ticket touches

steps.label: Trace one real request end to end
steps.detail: Go to definition, find references, and a breakpoint on a real request

steps.label: Search for anchors
steps.detail: An error message, URL path, config key or UI text: `rg "Payment declined"`

steps.label: Read the tests for that area
steps.detail: Intended behavior, and how to build the objects involved

steps.label: Ask the history why
steps.detail: `git log`, `git blame`, then the linked pull request and ticket

steps.label: Write down a map
steps.detail: Modules, data flow, a glossary of domain terms: docs for the next new hire

sections.code:
$ rg "Payment declined" --type py              # where does this error come from?
$ rg -n "def place_order|/orders" src/         # entry points for the feature
$ git log --oneline -- src/billing/invoice.py  # how this file evolved
$ git blame -L 120,140 src/billing/invoice.py  # which commit last changed these lines
$ git show 3f2a91c                             # that commit and its message: the why
$ pytest tests/billing -k invoice -x -q        # run the tests for this area
sections.pitfall: Trying to understand the whole system before changing anything. Follow one real request for your ticket, make a small change with a test, and let the map grow from there.

check.question: A line of code looks pointless and you want to delete it. What should you do first?
choices: Comment it out and leave it
Ask in the company-wide channel who wrote it
Delete it; the tests will catch any problem
Use git blame and the linked pull request or ticket to learn why it was added
check.explanation: History usually records the reason: a bug fix, a customer edge case, a workaround. Tests may not cover the case it protects, so understand it before removing it.

sections.title: Design docs and decision records
sections.key: Write a design doc before big or hard-to-undo work, share a rough draft early, and record why: goals, non-goals and the alternatives you rejected.
sections.body:
Before building something that takes more than a couple of weeks, involves several teams, or is hard to undo (a new service, a schema change, a new vendor), many companies expect a **design doc**, also called an RFC or tech spec.

Gaps show up in a document long before production, reviewers catch problems while change is cheap, and the doc records why.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Keep it as short as the problem allows; a few pages is typical. For smaller single decisions, many teams keep **architecture decision records (ADRs)**: short numbered files in the repository with context, decision and consequences, such as `docs/adr/0007-use-postgresql.md`.

As a junior you will mostly read and comment at first: ask clarifying questions and raise edge cases ("what happens when the queue is down?"). Writing a short doc for your first sizable project is one of the fastest ways to grow.

layers.label: Context and problem
layers.detail: What happens today, and why it must change

layers.label: Goals and non-goals
layers.detail: What success means, and what you deliberately will not solve: non-goals stop scope growth in review

layers.label: Proposed design
layers.detail: Components, data model, APIs, a diagram, how it fails

layers.label: Alternatives considered
layers.detail: And why they lost, so reviewers challenge the reasoning instead of re-proposing them

layers.label: Risks
layers.detail: Security, privacy, cost, performance, operational load

layers.label: Rollout
layers.detail: Feature flags, migrations and backfills, monitoring, how to roll back

layers.label: Open questions
layers.detail: Where you want reviewers to weigh in

steps.label: Share a rough draft early with one or two people
steps.detail: Before most of the work is built

steps.label: Revise, then circulate for written comments
Hold a design review if disagreements remain

sections.deeper: **A design doc in brief: accent-insensitive search (SEARCH-71).** Goals: match regardless of case and accents, with p95 latency under 300 ms. Non-goals: typo tolerance, ranking changes, stemming for other languages. Proposal: a `normalized_title` column (unaccent plus lower) filled by a batched backfill, with an index, and queries that compare normalized input. Alternatives: database collation (not supported by the managed version) and an external search engine (solves more but adds a service to run; revisit later). Rollout: behind the flag `search_normalized`; backfill 2 million rows in batches of 10,000; enable for staff, then 10%, then everyone. Rollback: turn the flag off, watching search latency and the zero-result rate. Open question: normalize authors' names in the same migration?
sections.pitfall: Writing the design doc after the code is done. Its value is getting feedback while changing direction is cheap; share a draft before you build.

check.question: Which section of a design doc lists what the project will deliberately not solve?
choices: Rollout
Non-goals
Open questions
Context
check.explanation: Non-goals set boundaries, so reviewers do not expand the scope and readers know what to expect. Open questions are things you want input on.

sections.title: Code review from both sides
sections.key: As an author, send small, well-described pull requests; as a reviewer, even a new one, review properly, say what you checked and respond within a day.
sections.body:
On the job, review is a workflow you manage every day, as author and as reviewer, and it sets how fast the whole team moves.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

**Turnaround matters**: a PR waiting three days blocks a teammate and invites merge conflicts. Many teams expect a first response within one working day; if you cannot manage that, say so, so the author can wait or ask someone else.

**Disagreements**: style goes to the linter or style guide, correctness gets evidence (a failing test, a benchmark), and preferences are the author's call. If a thread goes in circles:

[[visual 3]]

items.title: As the author
points: Small, focused PRs: one purpose, a few hundred changed lines at most. Reviewers catch far more in five 300-line diffs than one 1,500-line diff
Separate refactoring from behavior changes; split big features into **stacked** PRs or merge behind a feature flag
Review your own diff and get CI green first
Ask specific people: the code owner, or whoever knows the area

items.title: As a reviewer, even the newest
points: You should review: it is one of the fastest ways to learn the codebase
Read the description, then tests, edge cases, error handling, naming
Ask about anything you do not understand
Say what you checked and what you could not judge
Do not rubber-stamp: approve only code you would be comfortable debugging

visual.title: A PR description
rows: Ignore accents and case when searching titles and authors (linked ticket SEARCH-71)
"pokemon" does not find "Pokémon Red"; 14 support tickets in March
A `normalized_title` column with a batched backfill and an index, behind the flag `search_normalized`
Run the migrations and `pytest tests/search -q`; on staging, search "pokemon" with the flag on
Risks: the backfill takes about 4 minutes on staging. Not included: typo tolerance

steps.label: Reply in writing with your reasoning and evidence
Have a short call with the reviewer
Write the outcome of the call in the PR
Still stuck? Ask the tech lead to decide
Commit to the decision and move on

sections.pitfall: Opening a 2,000-line pull request that mixes a refactor, a feature and formatting changes. Reviewers skim it, bugs slip through, and it sits for days; split it.

check.question: You are the newest engineer, and a senior teammate asks you to review their PR. What is the most useful approach?
choices: Only check formatting
Approve immediately, since they are more experienced
Decline, because juniors should not review seniors
Review it properly, ask about anything unclear, and say which parts you could not judge
check.explanation: Questions from someone new expose unclear code, and reviewing teaches you the system. Being explicit about what you could not judge keeps the approval honest.

sections.title: Documentation people actually read
sections.key: Match each doc to what its reader needs (tutorial, how-to, reference or explanation), keep docs in the repository, and update them in the same pull request as the code.
sections.body:
Code nobody can run, change or fix at 3 a.m. is useless to the team. Documentation is how knowledge survives people leaving.

The **Diataxis** framework sorts docs by what the reader needs. Mixing the types is what makes docs hard to use: a reference page that turns into a tutorial serves neither reader.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Habits that keep docs alive:

- **Docs as code**: Markdown in the repository, reviewed in pull requests, and updated **in the same PR** as the change it describes.
- **Write for skimming**: headings, short paragraphs, commands that copy and paste.
- **Delete or mark outdated docs**: wrong docs are worse than none, because people trust them.

New hires are the best doc testers: fix whatever tripped you up in the README. It is the perfect first pull request.

visual.title: Diataxis
rows: Exact, complete facts, ideally generated from code
API docs from OpenAPI, CLI help, every config option
The why and the big picture

visual.title: What most teams need
rows: In every repository: what it is, how to run, test and deploy it, who owns it, where to get help
For each alert: what it means and its impact, how to confirm it, how to mitigate or fix it, when to escalate, links to dashboards and logs
Public functions documented; comments explain **why** ("skip weekends: the bank does not settle on Saturdays"), not what the next line does
The big picture and past decisions

sections.pitfall: Updating the code but not the docs that describe it. Make doc changes part of the same pull request, so reviewers see both and they cannot drift apart.

check.question: A page explains exactly which steps to follow to rotate the database password. Which Diataxis type is it?
choices: Explanation
Tutorial
How-to guide
Reference
check.explanation: A how-to guide is a recipe for one task for someone who already knows the basics. A tutorial teaches a newcomer by doing, and reference lists facts.

sections.title: Working with product managers and designers
sections.key: The PM owns the problem, the designer the experience, engineers how it is built; you add value by asking why, raising edge cases early and offering trade-offs instead of refusals.
sections.body:
Software is built by small cross-functional teams, and engineers who work well with the non-engineers on them get trusted with more.

[[visual]]

Strong teams decide together; weak teams pass documents over a wall. Habits that make you valuable:

- **Understand the problem, not just the spec**: what user need does it serve, and how will you know it worked?
- **Surface edge cases early**: empty, loading and error states, long names, slow networks, permissions, accessibility. In design they are cheap; after launch they are bugs.
- **Talk in trade-offs, not refusals**: scope, time and quality are the levers. Never silently cut quality.
- **Show work early**: release behind a feature flag to staff or a few users first: real behavior, limited risk, and off without a deploy.
- **Measure**: analytics events, dashboards, A/B tests.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Who owns what
rows: The problem: which user needs matter most, priorities, what not to build, and how success is measured
The experience: user research, flows, interaction and visual design, accessibility
How it is built (feasibility, architecture, quality, estimates), and partners on what gets built

visual.title: Trade-offs, not refusals
rows: "Basic filters can ship Friday. Saved filters need a new table and API, about 2 more weeks. Basic first, saved next sprint?"
"The live preview needs a request per keystroke. Could it update when typing pauses (300 ms)? It feels the same and costs far less."
"Shipped behind the flag for staff. Dashboard: filter usage and zero-result searches. 10% of users on Monday if numbers look fine."

sections.tip: Respect each other's expertise: the designer's choices come from research, the PM's priorities from customers. Explain your maintenance and reliability concerns in terms of user impact and cost.
sections.pitfall: Building exactly what the ticket says without asking why. You can deliver a perfect solution to the wrong problem; a five-minute conversation about the user's need often changes the design.

check.question: A PM asks for a feature you estimate at four weeks, but they need something in one. What is the most helpful response?
choices: Agree and hope to work faster
Offer options: a smaller version in one week, with what it leaves out, and the rest after
Ask your manager to tell the PM no
Refuse, since the estimate is four weeks
check.explanation: Trade-offs on scope turn a conflict into a decision the PM can make with full information. Overpromising or refusing both damage trust.

sections.title: Incidents and on-call: the human side
sections.key: In an incident, acknowledge and escalate early, split the roles, mitigate the impact before hunting the root cause, then learn from a blameless postmortem.
sections.body:
3:07 a.m. Your phone buzzes: checkout errors are at 30%. Shipping Code: CI/CD and the Cloud covers the alerts behind that page; this is what people do next.

**On-call**: engineers take turns, often a week at a time, as first responder, with a secondary and the service owners behind them. New engineers usually **shadow** first.

Acknowledge pages promptly, follow the **runbook**, and **escalate early** when out of your depth: that is the system working. End a shift with a **handoff note**: what fired, what you did, what is open.

[[visual]]

For anything serious (a high **severity**, such as SEV1), the team opens a channel and splits the work:

[[visual 2]]

**Mitigate before you diagnose**, and announce actions first ("rolling back deploy 482 now") so two people never change the same thing. In your first incidents, offer specific help and stay off the critical path.

visual.title: Handling an incident

steps.label: Mitigate the impact
steps.detail: Roll back the deploy, turn off the flag, fail over, add capacity, block an abusive client

steps.label: Resolve and monitor
steps.detail: Find and fix the root cause with the pressure off

steps.label: Write a blameless postmortem
steps.detail: Timeline, impact, causes and contributing factors, action items with owners. It asks how the system allowed the mistake, because blame makes people hide information

visual.caption: Started 03:04, paged 03:07, recovered 03:31 after a rollback: time to mitigate is 27 minutes from when the problem began.

visual.title: Roles
rows: Coordinates, sets priorities, assigns tasks; does not debug
Posts status updates to stakeholders on a fixed rhythm, such as every 30 minutes, even "still investigating"
Keeps the timeline of what was seen and done (or the channel does)
Written steps for handling a specific alert

sections.pitfall: Debugging the root cause while users are still affected. Mitigate first (roll back, disable the flag, fail over), then investigate calmly once the bleeding has stopped.

activity.title: Measure an incident's timeline
activity.prompt: Postmortems report how quickly each stage happened. Write a minutes() helper that turns "HH:MM" into minutes since midnight (datetime.strptime with "%H:%M"), then subtract the start time from the alert, acknowledgment, mitigation and resolution entries.

props.code:
from datetime import datetime

timeline = [
    ("03:04", "Checkout error rate passes 5%"),
    ("03:07", "Alert pages the on-call engineer"),
    ("03:11", "On-call acknowledges the page"),
    ("03:19", "Incident declared SEV2, channel opened"),
    ("03:26", "Deploy 482 rolled back"),
    ("03:31", "Error rate back below 0.5%: mitigated"),
    ("04:10", "Root cause found: a missing database index"),
    ("09:30", "Fix with the index deployed: resolved"),
]

# Measured in minutes from when the problem started (the first entry), print:
#   time to detect: N min       (until the alert paged)
#   time to acknowledge: N min  (until the page was acknowledged)
#   time to mitigate: N min     (until the error rate recovered)
#   time to resolve: N min      (until the incident was resolved)
for time, event in timeline:
    print(time, event)
props.task: Print time to detect: 3 min, time to acknowledge: 7 min, time to mitigate: 27 min and time to resolve: 386 min.
props.expectOutput:
time to detect: 3 min
time to acknowledge: 7 min
time to mitigate: 27 min
time to resolve: 386 min

check.question: Errors spiked right after a deploy 20 minutes ago, and you are on call. What is usually the first thing to do?
choices: Roll back the deploy (or turn off its feature flag) to stop the impact
Wait an hour to see if it recovers
Write the postmortem
Find the exact line that caused the bug before touching anything
check.explanation: Mitigation comes first: a rollback restores service in minutes, and the root cause can be found afterwards with the pressure off.

sections.title: Communication habits that build trust
sections.key: Give status without being asked, raise risks early with options, write messages that stand alone, close loops and keep a brag document.
sections.body:
Two engineers write equally good code. One gets the next big project. Very often the difference is communication: people know what the first one is doing, problems never surprise anyone, and promises are kept.

[[visual]]

A written update needs four parts:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Disagree openly and respectfully, with reasons, then support the decision once it is made. "Disagree and commit" is how teams move forward without pretending everyone agrees.

visual.title: Habits worth building
rows: Short, regular written updates; nobody should need to chase you
After 15 to 30 minutes (longer for big tasks), with context, what you tried and your best guess; in team channels, so answers help others
Question, context, links, urgency and deadline in one message; use threads
"The migration may lock the table for 4 hours. Run it Sunday night, or batch it over a week? I suggest batching."
Say when it is done; post the answer you found yourself
Come prepared; write down decisions and action items with owners
Bring an agenda: progress, blockers, feedback, career goals. Ask for specific feedback
What you shipped and its impact in numbers, what you learned, who you helped: gold at review time

visual.title: A Friday update
rows: Accent-insensitive search behind a flag (PR #482); staff testing since Wednesday
Production backfill Tuesday night; 10% of users Thursday
DBA approval for the backfill window (asked Priya on Wednesday)
The backfill could slow writes: batches of 10k, can pause at any time

items.title: Hello, then silence
points: "hi" (and nothing else)
Nothing to act on yet: the reader has to ask what you need

items.title: Stands alone
points: "I'm trying to run the payments service locally. `make dev` fails with 'connection refused' on port 5432. Docker is running and I followed the setup doc through step 4. I think the db container exits on start (logs attached). Is there a step I'm missing?"

sections.pitfall: Going quiet when stuck. Two silent days look like no progress at all; a short message with what you tried turns being stuck into a five-minute fix.

check.question: What is wrong with sending a teammate just "hi, got a minute?" and waiting?
choices: It should be sent as an email instead
It is rude to greet people
It forces a round trip before they know what you need; put the question and context in the first message
Messages should never contain questions
check.explanation: A self-contained message lets the reader answer whenever they are free, often in one reply. A bare greeting costs both of you a context switch and delays the answer.

sections.title: Growing from junior to mid-level
sections.key: Growing to mid-level means more scope, autonomy and ownership: owning features end to end with little guidance, through to results in production.
sections.body:
Titles differ between companies, but growth looks similar. Most companies publish a **career ladder**; read yours early, because it defines what "doing well" means there.

[[visual]]

The step from junior to mid is a change in three things:

[[visual 2]]

How to get there, deliberately:

- Ask your manager where you stand and what evidence would show you are operating at the next level.
- Ask for slightly bigger, vaguer work. Volunteer for incidents, migrations, on-call and design docs: messy work teaches fastest.
- Learn the domain: users, how the product makes money, which metrics matter. Go deep in one area while learning the systems around it.
- Make impact visible (demos, write-ups, a brag document) and help others (onboarding docs, reviews).
- Keep a sustainable pace: reliable delivery beats heroics.

Promotions usually recognize work you have already been doing at the next level for a while.

visual.title: Levels, roughly
rows: Well-defined tasks, with guidance; learning the codebase, tools and practices; asking good questions
Features end to end with little guidance: clarifies, designs, builds, tests, ships and monitors. Reviews usefully, takes on-call alone
Projects across people and teams, technical direction; anticipates problems and makes others more effective

visual.title: Junior to mid
rows: A feature, then a small project
Being told what, then finding what needs doing
"It works in production and users got what they needed": you check the dashboards after release and fix what you find

sections.deeper:
**A brag document, one quarter.** Shipped: accent-insensitive search (SEARCH-71), with zero-result searches down 18% and search support tickets down from 14 to 2 a month; wrote the design doc. Cut the CI pipeline from 14 to 6 minutes by caching dependencies and splitting slow tests. Operations: first solo on-call week; led the mitigation of a checkout incident (rollback in 9 minutes) and wrote the postmortem, with 3 of 4 action items done. Helping others: rewrote the local setup README, so two new hires set up in a day instead of three; reviewed 41 pull requests. Learning: PostgreSQL query plans, and a 20-minute team talk on EXPLAIN.

Promotions for juniors often come a year or two after joining. The work comes first; the title follows.
sections.pitfall: Waiting to be handed bigger work. Growth usually comes from volunteering for the next size of problem and asking your manager what evidence the next level needs.

check.question: What best describes the shift from junior to mid-level engineer?
choices: Owning features end to end with little guidance, from unclear requirements to results in production
Managing other engineers
Knowing more programming languages
Writing code faster
check.explanation: Mid-level is about scope, autonomy and ownership of outcomes. Speed and languages help, and people management is a separate track.

keyTerms.definition: An approach to software development that delivers in small increments, gathers feedback early and adapts the plan.
In scrum, a fixed period (often two weeks) in which the team completes a planned set of backlog items.
The ordered list of work a team might do, with the most valuable items at the top.
A cap on how many items may be in a kanban column at once, used to expose bottlenecks and keep work flowing.
How long one work item takes from start to done.
Concrete, checkable conditions that define when a ticket is done.
A relative estimate of size that combines effort, complexity and uncertainty.
A thin piece of a feature that works end to end through every layer, so it can be shipped and tested.
A short, time-boxed investigation that answers an unknown before work is estimated or committed.
A written proposal (also called an RFC) describing a problem, goals, design, alternatives and rollout, reviewed before building.
A short document in the repository recording one significant decision, its context and its consequences.
Written steps for handling a specific alert or operational task.
A written incident review that focuses on how systems and processes allowed a failure, not on who to blame.
The person who coordinates an incident response: sets priorities and assigns tasks rather than debugging.
A schedule in which engineers take turns being the first responder to alerts for a set of services.
A running personal record of work shipped, impact, learning and help given, used for reviews and promotions.

summary: Agile teams work in small batches: scrum through sprints, kanban through WIP limits; most mix both.
Tickets need acceptance criteria; slice work vertically and update estimates early.
Learn a codebase by running it, tracing a real request, searching anchors and reading history.
Design docs get feedback before building; small, well-described PRs get fast reviews.
In incidents, mitigate first, split the roles, then hold a blameless postmortem.
Visible status, early risks and a brag document build trust; mid-level means more scope and ownership.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who is about to start their first engineering job what happens in a typical two-week sprint, from planning to retro, and what they personally should do each day to be seen as reliable.

questions.question: Match each scrum event with its purpose.

pairs.right: Choose the work and goal for the next sprint
Coordinate: progress, plans and blockers in about 15 minutes
Demo what was built and gather stakeholder feedback
Clarify, split and estimate upcoming items

questions.explanation: Each event has one job. When a meeting drifts from its job (a standup that becomes a design debate), the team loses time.

questions.question: What is the main difference between scrum and kanban?
choices: Kanban has no board
Scrum has no planning
Kanban requires a scrum master
Scrum works in fixed-length sprints; kanban is a continuous flow limited by work-in-progress limits
questions.explanation: Scrum commits to a batch of work per sprint. Kanban pulls work continuously and controls flow with WIP limits, which suits unpredictable incoming work.

questions.question: What are cycle time and throughput on a kanban team?
questions.answer: Cycle time is how long one item takes from start to done. Throughput is how many items the team finishes per period, such as per week.
questions.explanation: Together they describe flow. Long cycle times usually mean items are too big or waiting, often in review; limiting work in progress shortens them.

questions.question: Which habits help your team from your first week? Select all that apply.
choices: Keep your tickets' status current on the board
Mention a blocker at the next standup instead of waiting
Start several tickets at once so you always have something to do
Finish and ship one item before pulling the next
Save problems for the retro at the end of the sprint
questions.explanation: Visible status, early blockers and finishing before starting keep work flowing. Many open tickets and late surprises do the opposite.

questions.question: What is the biggest problem with this ticket?
questions.code:
Title: Improve the export
Description: The export should be
better. Users have complained.
choices: The title is too short
It has no context or acceptance criteria, so nobody can tell what done means
It should be assigned to a manager
It needs a story point estimate first
questions.explanation: Without the problem (which complaint, which users) and checkable criteria (CSV includes the date column; exports of 50,000 rows finish in under 10 seconds), the work cannot be estimated, built or verified.

questions.question: Halfway through a 3-day ticket, you discover it needs a database migration nobody planned. What should you do?
choices: Skip the migration and hope it works
Wait until the deadline to mention it
Work evenings so the estimate stays right
Tell the team now what you found and your new estimate
questions.explanation: Early updates let the team re-plan while there are still options. Hidden overtime and late surprises erode trust far more than a revised estimate.

questions.question: What is a spike, and when do you propose one?
questions.answer: A short, time-boxed investigation that answers an unknown (can this library do X, how slow is this query) before committing to an estimate. Propose one when unknowns dominate a task.
questions.explanation: A spike turns "no idea, maybe a week" into a real estimate after half a day. Its output is knowledge and a recommendation, not production code.

questions.question: Which items are commonly forgotten when estimating a ticket? Select all that apply.
choices: Writing and fixing tests
Code review rounds
Database migrations and backfills
Updating documentation
Typing speed
questions.explanation: Coding is often less than half the work. Typing speed is never the bottleneck; understanding, testing, reviewing and shipping are.

questions.question: Show which commit last changed each of lines 120 to 140 of src/billing/invoice.py.
questions.explanation: git blame with -L limits the output to a line range and shows the commit, author and date for each line. git show <commit> then displays the change and its message.

questions.question: You are new to a codebase and need to change how invoices are numbered. Put a sensible approach in order.
items: Get the project running locally with its tests passing
Search for where invoice numbers are created
Trace one real invoice creation in the debugger
Read the existing tests for that code
Make a small change with a new test
questions.explanation: Run it, find the entry point, watch it execute, learn the intended behavior from tests, then change it safely. Each step narrows what you need to understand.

questions.question: Which question to a teammate is most likely to get a fast, useful answer?
choices: "How does billing work?"
"Nothing works, can you help?"
"I traced the invoice number to InvoiceService.next_number, but staging shows gaps. Is that expected from the retry job?"
"Who wrote this code?"
questions.explanation: A specific question with what you tried and a hypothesis can be answered in a minute. Broad questions need a meeting, and vague ones need a round of questions back first.

questions.question: What is the name of the principle that you should understand why something exists before removing it? (Two words, the first is a surname.)
questions.explanation: G. K. Chesterton's parable: if you find a fence across a road and see no use for it, go and find out why it was built before you tear it down.

questions.question: Which projects usually deserve a design doc? Select all that apply.
choices: Splitting a monolith's billing code into its own service
Changing the primary key type of the orders table
Fixing a typo in an error message
Adopting a new third-party payment provider
Renaming a local variable
questions.explanation: Design docs pay off for work that is large, crosses teams or is hard to reverse. Small, easily reverted changes just need a good pull request description.
questions.concept: when to write a design doc

questions.question: Why is "Alternatives considered" one of the most valuable sections of a design doc?
choices: It makes the document longer
It shows the options weighed and why they lost, so reviewers can challenge the reasoning instead of re-proposing them
It is required by law
It lists which engineers disagreed
questions.explanation: Without it, every reviewer asks "why not X?". With it, the discussion focuses on whether the trade-offs were judged correctly.

questions.question: What is an architecture decision record (ADR)?
questions.answer: A short, numbered document in the repository recording one significant decision: its context, the decision and its consequences.
questions.explanation: ADRs are cheap to write and keep the reasons behind decisions next to the code, where future maintainers will find them.

questions.question: When should you share the first draft of a design doc?
choices: Early, as a rough draft with one or two people, before most of the work is built
Only after the implementation is finished
Never; design docs are for managers
After every section is polished, to the whole company at once
questions.explanation: Feedback is cheapest before code exists. A rough draft to a couple of knowledgeable people catches big problems before you polish the wrong design.

questions.question: A feature needs about 1,200 lines of changes. What makes it easiest to review?
choices: Commit straight to main and review later
One PR, so reviewers see everything at once
Several small, focused PRs (stacked or behind a feature flag), each with its own description
One PR without a description, to save time
questions.explanation: Small PRs get faster, more careful reviews and are easier to revert. A feature flag lets incomplete pieces merge safely.

questions.question: Which belong in a good pull request description? Select all that apply.
choices: What changed and why
How to test it
Risks or anything reviewers should look at closely
A link to the ticket
The full contents of every changed file
questions.explanation: The description gives reviewers context the diff cannot: intent, verification and risk. The diff itself already shows the file contents.

questions.question: A review thread about your change is going in circles. Put the escalation steps in order.
items: Reply in writing with your reasoning and evidence
Have a short call with the reviewer
Write the outcome of the call in the PR
If still stuck, ask the tech lead to decide
Commit to the decision and move on
questions.explanation: Most disagreements end at the first or second step. Recording the outcome keeps everyone aligned, and committing to a decision you argued against is a mark of professionalism.

questions.question: A teammate's pull request has waited two days for your review, and you are busy until tomorrow afternoon. What is best?
choices: Tell them you cannot get to it until tomorrow afternoon, so they can wait or ask someone else
Ask them to close it and open a new one
Say nothing and review it when you can
Approve it without reading so they are unblocked
questions.explanation: Silence blocks the author with no way to plan. A quick note keeps them in control, while a blind approval defeats the point of review.

questions.question: Match each document with the Diataxis category it belongs to.

pairs.left: A step-by-step first project for new users
How to restore a database backup
Every configuration option with its type and default
Why the system uses event sourcing

questions.explanation: Each type answers a different reader need: learning, doing a task, looking something up, or understanding.

questions.question: What is the best moment to update the documentation for a behavior change?
choices: At the end of the quarter
Only when someone complains
After the next release
In the same pull request as the code change
questions.explanation: Docs in the same PR are reviewed together with the code, so they ship together and cannot drift. Later almost always becomes never.

questions.question: What should a runbook for an alert contain?
questions.answer: What the alert means and its impact, how to confirm it, the steps to mitigate or fix it, and when and how to escalate, with links to dashboards and logs.
questions.explanation: A runbook lets whoever is on call act quickly at 3 a.m. without being the expert on that system.

questions.question: Which code comment adds the most value?
choices: # loop over the orders
# Retry once: the bank API drops the first request after being idle (see BANK-231)
# TODO
# increment the counter
questions.explanation: Good comments explain why the code is the way it is, which the code itself cannot say. Comments that repeat the code add noise and go stale.

questions.question: Who usually owns which user problem to solve next and how success will be measured?
choices: The designer
The newest engineer
The database administrator
The product manager
questions.explanation: PMs own the what and why, designers the experience, engineers the how. All three contribute to decisions, but priorities sit with product.

questions.question: Which edge cases are worth raising with a designer before building a profile page? Select all that apply.
choices: A user with no profile photo
A name that is 60 characters long
The page while data is still loading
What happens when the API returns an error
The color of the company logo in last year's brand guide
questions.explanation: Empty, long, loading and error states are the gaps designs most often miss. Settling them early is cheap; discovering them in QA means rework.

questions.question: Why release a new feature behind a feature flag to internal users or a small percentage first?
questions.answer: It lets the team see real behavior and metrics with limited risk, and turn the feature off instantly without a deploy if something goes wrong.
questions.explanation: Flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature. They make demos, experiments and quick rollbacks possible.

questions.question: Put the stages of handling an incident in order.
questions.explanation: Detection to postmortem; mitigation comes before full root-causing, and the postmortem turns the incident into lasting improvements.

questions.question: An incident began at 03:04, the alert paged at 03:07, and the error rate recovered at 03:31 after a rollback. What was the time to mitigate, measured from when the problem began, in minutes?
questions.explanation: 03:31 minus 03:04 is 27 minutes. Users care most about this number: the root cause was found later, but they were no longer affected.

questions.question: What makes a postmortem blameless?
choices: It is never shared outside the team
Nobody is allowed to mention what happened
It focuses on how the system and process allowed the failure, not on punishing a person
Only managers may write it
questions.explanation: When people are not afraid of blame, they share what really happened, and the fixes target the real causes, such as missing checks or confusing tools.

questions.question: Match each incident role or tool with its job.

pairs.right: Coordinates, sets priorities and assigns tasks; does not debug
Posts regular status updates to stakeholders
Keeps the timeline of what was seen and done
Written steps for handling a specific alert

questions.explanation: Separating coordination, communication and investigation keeps a stressful incident orderly. The timeline then feeds the postmortem.

questions.question: You are shadowing your first on-call week and an alert fires that the runbook does not cover. What should you do?
choices: Stay quiet and keep reading logs alone
Tell the primary on-call what you see and ask how to help, following your team's escalation process
Restart random services to see if it helps
Silence the alert until morning
questions.explanation: Escalating early is how on-call is supposed to work. Unannounced changes and silenced alerts turn small incidents into big ones.

questions.question: Which belong in a good written status update? Select all that apply.
choices: What you finished
What you will do next
What is blocking you and who can unblock it
Risks you see coming
Every command you ran this week
questions.explanation: Done, next, blocked and risks tell readers everything they need in under a minute. Raw activity logs bury the signal.

questions.question: This message is likely to get a slow or unhelpful reply. What is the main problem?
choices: It contains no question or context, so the reader cannot help until another round trip
It should mention their manager
It uses lowercase
It is too informal
questions.explanation: Include the question, what you tried, links and urgency in the first message, so the reader can answer the moment they see it.

questions.question: What is a brag document, and why keep one?
questions.answer: A running list of what you shipped, its measurable impact, what you learned and who you helped. It makes performance reviews and promotion cases accurate, because everyone forgets details over months.
questions.explanation: Update it weekly in a few minutes. It also feeds your resume and your interview stories (Behavioral Interviews).

questions.question: Which behavior most clearly shows ownership of outcomes?
choices: Asking for the requirements to be fully written before starting
Closing the ticket as soon as the PR merges
Checking the dashboards after release, finding a slow query and fixing it
Waiting for QA to report problems
questions.explanation: Owning the outcome means caring that users got the result, not only that code merged. Following up in production is the clearest signal.

questions.question: Which actions help a junior engineer grow toward mid-level? Select all that apply.
choices: Asking your manager what evidence the next level needs
Volunteering for an on-call rotation and incident follow-ups
Avoiding ambiguous tasks until you feel ready
Keeping a brag document
Improving onboarding docs for the next new hire
questions.explanation: Clear expectations, messy real-world work, visible impact and helping others all build the case. Avoiding ambiguity avoids exactly the skill that defines the next level.

questions.question: Match each level with the scope it typically owns.

pairs.right: Features end to end, with little guidance
Projects across people and teams, and technical direction

questions.explanation: Each step widens the scope and the ambiguity you handle on your own. Ladders differ in detail, but this progression is nearly universal.
